title: How a dbt Project Reaches Fabric Data Warehouse
purpose: Trace a dbt project from local development through the dbt-fabric adapter, Entra ID auth, and CTAS-based T-SQL translation, to a running debug/seed/run/test cycle and scheduled Airflow orchestration.
accessibleSummary: An architecture flow with seven steps. A dbt project's profiles.yml declares Fabric as its target via the dbt-fabric adapter, which authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID — interactively for development, via service principal for automation. The adapter translates dbt's usual ALTER/MERGE/TRUNCATE-style operations into CREATE TABLE AS SELECT plus DROP/CREATE sequences because Fabric's T-SQL surface doesn't support the same commands SQL Server does. Running debug, seed, run, and test against the jaffle_shop sample project validates the connection end to end. Production scheduling is handled outside dbt itself, by pairing dbt with Apache Airflow inside Fabric Data Factory. A warning node flags that this is a third-party adapter, not a native Fabric feature, so its translation gaps are the adapter's problem to work around, not Fabric's to fix.
longDescription: This flow starts at a dbt project on a developer's machine and ends at a production Airflow-orchestrated schedule triggering dbt runs against Fabric Warehouse. In between it shows the concrete mechanics documented by Microsoft: profiles.yml configuration switches the target to Fabric via the dbt-fabric PyPI adapter (a third-party package, not a Fabric-native integration); authentication is Microsoft Entra ID based, using interactive az login for day-to-day development and a service principal for unattended production runs; and because Fabric Warehouse's T-SQL surface doesn't support the full SQL Server command set dbt models assume, the adapter works around operations like ALTER TABLE, MERGE, TRUNCATE, and sp_rename by translating them into CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) plus DROP/CREATE sequences instead. The validation cycle — dbt debug, seed, run, test — is demonstrated end to end against the open-source jaffle_shop sample project. Because dbt itself has no native scheduler, Fabric documents pairing it with Apache Airflow inside Data Factory for recurring production runs. A dedicated warning node makes explicit that this whole path runs through a third-party, Microsoft-org-maintained open-source adapter, not a first-party Fabric capability — so adapter-specific issues are filed on GitHub, not through Fabric support.

nodes.label: dbt project (local/CI)
nodes.summary: A standard dbt project authored and run from outside Fabric, via VS Code/CLI.
nodes.detail: The dbt project itself — models, tests, profiles.yml — is authored and driven entirely outside Fabric, from a developer's machine or a CI runner, using the standard dbt CLI. Nothing about the project structure changes to target Fabric; only the profiles.yml connection configuration does.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because dbt itself lives outside Fabric, the project's version control, review process, and CI pipeline are whatever the team already uses for dbt elsewhere — Fabric doesn't introduce a new authoring surface here.

evidence.note: The adapter is installed and driven from outside Fabric (VS Code/CLI), requiring Python, the Microsoft ODBC Driver for SQL Server, and a SQL analytics endpoint connection string.

inputs: dbt models, tests, and a profiles.yml file
Python 3.7+, the Microsoft ODBC Driver for SQL Server, and an existing Fabric Warehouse
processing: Install the dbt-fabric adapter with pip install dbt-fabric
Author models and tests using standard dbt conventions
outputs: A dbt project ready to connect to Fabric Warehouse once profiles.yml is configured
drill.example: A team already running dbt against Snowflake installs dbt-fabric alongside their existing dbt-core install to evaluate targeting a Fabric Warehouse for a new project.
controls: Which Python/ODBC driver versions are installed on the dev machine or CI runner
failureModes: Missing the Microsoft ODBC Driver for SQL Server prerequisite and failing to connect with an unclear error

nodes.label: dbt-fabric adapter (PyPI)
nodes.summary: A third-party Python package that lets dbt target Fabric Warehouse via profiles.yml.
nodes.detail: Fabric Warehouse is supported as a dbt target through the dbt-fabric adapter, a Python package published on PyPI and installed with pip install dbt-fabric — not through any Fabric-native dbt integration. Moving between supported warehouse platforms (for example, an Azure Synapse dedicated SQL pool project moving to Fabric) is a three-step process: install the target adapter, change the type value in profiles.yml, and rebuild the project, with no model rewrite implied.
nodes.whyItMatters: Recognizing this is a third-party adapter, not a Fabric feature, sets the right expectation for support: adapter bugs are filed against the adapter's GitHub repo, not Fabric support.

evidence.note: Fabric Data Warehouse is supported as a dbt target via the dbt-fabric adapter, a Python package published on PyPI and installed with pip install dbt-fabric, rather than through a Fabric-native dbt integration.

Moving an existing dbt project between supported warehouse platforms is a three-step process: install the target platform's adapter, change the type value in profiles.yml, and rebuild the project — no model rewrite is implied.

inputs: A profiles.yml output block with type: fabric, the SQL analytics endpoint host, database/schema names, an ODBC driver string, and an auth mode
processing: The adapter translates dbt's generic materialization and test logic into Fabric-compatible T-SQL calls over the ODBC connection
outputs: A live connection from the dbt project to the target Fabric Warehouse's SQL analytics endpoint
drill.example: A project previously targeting Azure Synapse changes only the type field in profiles.yml from synapse to fabric and reinstalls the corresponding adapter, with model files untouched.
controls: The profiles.yml output block configuration: host, database, schema, driver, and auth mode
failureModes: Assuming the adapter is Microsoft first-party support rather than a community/Microsoft-org open-source project with its own issue tracker

nodes.label: Microsoft Entra ID authentication
nodes.summary: Interactive az login for development, service principal for automated runs.
nodes.detail: Fabric recommends Microsoft Entra ID authentication for dbt-fabric connections: interactive CLI-based authentication via az login for day-to-day development work, and service principal authentication for unattended, automated dbt runs such as a scheduled production job.
nodes.whyItMatters: Choosing the right auth mode per context matters because interactive az login isn't viable in an unattended pipeline, and using a personal interactive login for production automation is both fragile and a security anti-pattern.

evidence.note: Fabric recommends Microsoft Entra ID authentication for dbt-fabric connections: interactive CLI-based authentication (via az login) for day-to-day development work, and service principal authentication for unattended/automated dbt runs.

inputs: A developer's Entra ID credentials (development) or a registered service principal's credentials (automation)
processing: Development: authenticate interactively via az login before running dbt commands
Automation: configure the service principal's client ID/secret or certificate in the profiles.yml auth block
outputs: An authenticated ODBC connection to the Fabric Warehouse SQL analytics endpoint
drill.example: A developer runs az login once per day before iterating on dbt models locally, while the production Airflow DAG authenticates using a dedicated service principal with least-privilege access to just the target warehouse.
controls: Which auth mode is configured per environment (dev vs CI/production)
Least-privilege scoping of the service principal used for automation
failureModes: Hardcoding a developer's personal credentials into a CI pipeline instead of provisioning a service principal

nodes.label: CTAS-based T-SQL translation
nodes.summary: The adapter rewrites ALTER/MERGE/TRUNCATE-style operations as CTAS plus DROP/CREATE.
nodes.detail: The dbt-fabric adapter implements certain T-SQL operations dbt models rely on — including behaviors equivalent to ALTER TABLE ADD/ALTER/DROP COLUMN, MERGE, TRUNCATE, and sp_rename — by translating them into CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) plus DROP/CREATE sequences, because Fabric Data Warehouse's T-SQL surface does not support the same command set as SQL Server. dbt projects targeting Fabric are also subject to Fabric's general T-SQL command and data-type limitations, which apply platform-wide, not just to dbt.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the single most consequential architectural fact about targeting Fabric with dbt: models that assume SQL Server's full ALTER/MERGE semantics will still work, but through a rewrite-and-replace pattern rather than in-place mutation, which has different locking and cost characteristics.

evidence.note: The dbt-fabric adapter implements certain T-SQL operations dbt models rely on — including behaviors equivalent to ALTER TABLE ADD/ALTER/DROP COLUMN, MERGE, TRUNCATE, and sp_rename — by translating them into CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) plus DROP/CREATE sequences, because Fabric Data Warehouse's T-SQL surface does not support the same command set as SQL Server.

dbt projects targeting Fabric Warehouse are subject to Fabric Data Warehouse's general T-SQL command limitations and unsupported data types for tables; these are the same platform-wide constraints that apply outside of dbt, not adapter-specific restrictions.

inputs: A dbt model materialization or schema change that would normally issue ALTER, MERGE, TRUNCATE, or sp_rename in SQL Server
processing: The adapter detects the operation and rewrites it as a CTAS producing a new table
Old table is dropped and the new one renamed/created in its place
outputs: The same logical result as the original operation, achieved via rewrite-and-replace rather than in-place mutation
drill.example: A dbt incremental model that would issue a MERGE against SQL Server instead has the adapter build a new combined table via CTAS from the old table plus new rows, then swap it in for the original.
controls: Awareness that this rewrite pattern has different cost/locking characteristics than a true in-place MERGE, which matters for very large incremental models
failureModes: Assuming dbt-fabric MERGE incrementals behave identically in cost/locking to a native SQL Server MERGE, when the underlying mechanism is actually CTAS-based

nodes.label: debug / seed / run / test cycle
nodes.summary: The standard dbt validation workflow, demonstrated against the jaffle_shop sample project.
nodes.detail: The standard dbt-fabric validation workflow after configuring profiles.yml is dbt debug (test connectivity), dbt seed (load sample/seed data), dbt run (execute models), and dbt test (validate data against tests) — demonstrated end-to-end against Fabric Warehouse using the open-source jaffle_shop demo project.
nodes.whyItMatters: This cycle is the concrete proof that the CTAS translation and auth configuration actually work end to end before a team commits real production models to the connection.

evidence.note: The standard dbt-fabric validation workflow after configuring profiles.yml is dbt debug (test connectivity), dbt seed (load sample/seed data), dbt run (execute models), and dbt test (validate data against tests), demonstrated end-to-end against Fabric Warehouse using the open-source jaffle_shop demo project.

inputs: A configured profiles.yml pointing at a target Fabric Warehouse
processing: dbt seed loads sample CSV data into warehouse tables
dbt run executes model SQL as CTAS-translated statements
dbt test validates results against defined data tests
outputs: A validated end-to-end connection with sample data proving the full cycle works
drill.example: A team new to dbt-fabric runs the jaffle_shop tutorial end to end — debug, seed, run, test — before writing a single production model, confirming the ODBC connection and CTAS translation both work correctly.
controls: Running this full cycle against a non-production warehouse first
failureModes: Skipping dbt debug and discovering an auth or driver misconfiguration only when dbt run fails midway through a real model set

nodes.label: Airflow orchestration in Data Factory
nodes.summary: Scheduled dbt runs are operationalized via Apache Airflow inside Fabric Data Factory, not a native dbt scheduler.
nodes.detail: Fabric documents operationalizing scheduled dbt runs by pairing dbt with Apache Airflow inside Fabric Data Factory, using Airflow's DAG-based scheduling and task orchestration to trigger dbt runs on a recurring basis, rather than via any native dbt scheduler in Fabric — dbt itself has no built-in production scheduler.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the piece a team new to Fabric might expect to be native and isn't; production dbt scheduling requires standing up an Airflow DAG rather than configuring a Fabric-native trigger.

evidence.note: Fabric documents operationalizing scheduled dbt runs by pairing dbt with Apache Airflow inside Fabric Data Factory, using Airflow's DAG-based scheduling and task orchestration to trigger dbt runs on a recurring basis, rather than via a native dbt scheduler in Fabric.

inputs: A validated dbt project ready for recurring production execution
processing: Define an Airflow DAG inside Fabric Data Factory that triggers dbt run/test tasks on a schedule
Use the service-principal auth mode configured earlier for the unattended run
outputs: Recurring, scheduled production dbt runs against the Fabric Warehouse, orchestrated and monitored via Airflow
drill.example: A nightly Airflow DAG in Data Factory triggers dbt run followed by dbt test against the production warehouse at 2 AM, alerting the data engineering team if the test step fails.
controls: DAG schedule cadence and failure-alerting configuration
failureModes: Expecting a native Fabric pipeline trigger to run dbt directly, when Airflow is the documented path for this

nodes.label: Third-party adapter, not a Fabric feature
nodes.summary: dbt-fabric is a Microsoft-org open-source project; adapter issues go to its GitHub repo, not Fabric support.
nodes.detail: The dbt-fabric adapter is maintained as an open-source project on GitHub under the microsoft org, where users are directed to file adapter-specific issues rather than through general Fabric support channels. This whole architecture — from profiles.yml through CTAS translation to Airflow scheduling — depends on this third-party layer staying compatible with both dbt-core and Fabric's evolving T-SQL surface.
nodes.whyItMatters: A team treating dbt-fabric as an official first-party Fabric feature will be surprised when an adapter bug requires a GitHub issue and a community fix cycle rather than a Microsoft support ticket with an SLA.

evidence.note: The dbt-fabric adapter is maintained as an open-source project on GitHub under the microsoft org, where users are directed to file adapter-specific issues rather than through general Fabric support channels.

inputs: A dbt-fabric adapter bug or unsupported-operation error encountered in production
processing: Distinguish whether the issue is a Fabric platform limitation (Fabric support) or an adapter translation bug (GitHub issue)
File the issue against the correct channel
outputs: An issue routed to whichever party can actually fix it, instead of stalling in the wrong support queue
drill.example: A team hits an unexpected CTAS translation error on a specific incremental model pattern and, recognizing the adapter is community-maintained, files a GitHub issue against the dbt-fabric repo rather than waiting on a Fabric support ticket.
controls: Document internally which support channel owns adapter-layer issues before the team hits its first one in production
failureModes: Escalating an adapter bug through Fabric support and waiting on a resolution that can only come from the open-source project
Pinning to an outdated adapter version indefinitely to avoid regressions, and missing fixes for known translation gaps
